source.title: Quantifying the generalization error in deep learning in terms of data distribution and neural network smoothness
source.authors: Peng-Zhan Jin; Lu Lu; Yi-Fa Tang; G. Karniadakis

record.file_problem: The supplied text is a complete paper, including appendices and references.
record.tranche_reason: The study numerically examines how data distribution and a smoothness measure relate to classification error and test loss, using methods different from the claim versions. It does not directly test the versions’ specified interventions or measures.
record.gate_note: The random-label experiment reports cover-complexity values only; it does not report training or test performance for random labels. Table K.3 reports cited here as individual training results, so its best-error entries are not extracted separately from the aggregate best errors in Table 1.
record.test_reason: The study tests its own cover-complexity and input-smoothness account of generalization, but none of V1–V8. Random labels receive no training/test performance evaluation; width comparisons lack interpolation or convergence evidence; convolutional features are not a CNN-versus-fully-connected comparison; input smoothness is not magnitude-aware weight sharpness.
record.authors_conclusion: The record is broadly accurate. More precisely, the authors derive conditional accuracy/error bounds involving cover complexity and input smoothness, report an approximately linear association between cover complexity and selected best error normalized by the square root of class count, and observe that greater smoothness accompanies lower test loss. They report decreasing smoothness with depth and width, little dependence on training-set size, and propose smoothness-based early stopping.
record.recipe_differences: The paper proposes and evaluates cover complexity and inverse-modulus smoothness, rather than testing the claim versions’ interventions or magnitude-aware sharpness. Fully connected networks use Adam in the reported experiments; architecture and learning rates are varied for best-error results.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported outcomes vary with dataset and dataset variant; measured smoothness decreases with network depth and width, with depth having the larger effect. Smoothness is reported as insensitive to training dataset size.

fits_no_version.finding: Across dataset variants, selected best fully connected test errors approximately track cover complexity; dividing error by the square root of class count yields a reported fitted relationship with R² approximately .92.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Cover complexity correlates with selected best classification error across the tested datasets and representations.

fits_no_version.finding: Normalized inverse-modulus smoothness decreases with depth and width and is reported as insensitive to training-set size in synthetic binary problems.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Under smoothness-based early stopping, the tested fully connected networks exhibit architecture-dependent input smoothness that changes little with training-set size.

fits_no_version.finding: Figures 5 and 6 associate lower test loss with greater input smoothness during training; the MNIST experiment uses a spectral-norm-based smoothness bound.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Input smoothness or its estimated bound tracks test loss during the tested training trajectories.

fits_no_version.finding: Across 50 random relabelings of MNIST, the smallest absolute cover complexity is approximately 300, versus less than 20 for the natural-label datasets; classifier performance is not measured.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The proposed cover-complexity statistic distinguishes random-label MNIST from the tested natural-label datasets.

record.problems: Best errors are selected across several tested network structures and learning rates; the text does not give uncertainty for Table 1. Smoothness results are presented in figures and described as averages over 50 experiments, without numerical uncertainty estimates. The random-label experiment reports cover complexity but no classifier performance.
record.rows_left_out: No results omitted from Table 1. The individual entries in Appendix K, Table K.3 are not extracted because Table 1 reports the best error aggregate for each dataset variant, and the architecture/learning-rate mapping in Table K.4 does not provide an additional claim-version outcome.

untested.parts: Coexistence of random-label fitting and natural-label generalization under the same recipe, including chance-level random-label held-out accuracy. Only random-label cover complexity is reported.
Test-error behavior beyond the width required for zero training error. Appendix K compares widths 256 and 512, but establishes neither interpolation nor training to convergence.
CNN-versus-fully-connected held-out performance and the contribution of local connectivity. Learned CNN features are compared with raw inputs to fully connected classifiers.
Adaptive-optimizer versus SGD generalization under controlled tuning. Different optimizers used in different pipeline stages provide no such comparison.
Large-versus-small batch generalization under matched epoch budgets and adapted recipes.
Dropout's effect on held-out error. Dropout in the feature-generating CNN is not ablated.
Magnitude-aware weight-perturbation sharpness, its association with generalization gaps, and its ranking against norm and margin measures. The measured smoothness concerns changes in inputs.
Accuracy after removing highly memorized examples versus equally many random examples.

record.verdict_notes: T6 applies relative to the supplied versions, despite substantive experiments on generalization more broadly. R1–R15 are descriptive selected-best summaries rather than independent claim tests. No absent or reversed version effect can be inferred from their lack of relevant comparisons.

versions.untested_parts: No random-label training fit or held-out accuracy is reported.
The width experiment measures smoothness, not test error across widths relative to the interpolation threshold.
No comparison of convolutional and fully connected networks trained from scratch is reported.
No adaptive-optimizer versus SGD comparison is reported.
Dropout is part of the CNN used to generate convolutional features, but dropout is not ablated.
The paper measures inverse-modulus smoothness, not magnitude-aware sharpness or its ranking against norm- and margin-based measures.
No training-example removal experiment is reported.
